sessions.title: Welcome: the road to Emmaus
sessions.summary: Every journey of faith starts with Jesus walking beside us, often before we recognize him.
lesson: On the first Easter Sunday, two disciples walked home from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles away. They were sad and confused: Jesus had died, and they did not understand the news that he was alive.

A stranger joined them on the road. He listened to them, then explained the Scriptures, showing how everything pointed to Jesus. When they reached the village they begged him, "Stay with us." At supper he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them. Their eyes were opened: it was Jesus.

Later they said to each other, "Were not our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us on the way?" That is the heart of this journey. You will hear the Scriptures, ask questions, walk with others, and come to the table of the Eucharist. Jesus is already walking with you, even on the days you do not see him.
You do not need to have everything figured out. The disciples on the road were full of doubts. Bring your questions; that is what this time is for.
sessions.reflection: What brought you to begin this journey? What are you hoping to find?

sessions.title: Prayer: talking with God
sessions.summary: Prayer is simply a conversation with God who loves you. Anyone can start today.
lesson: Prayer is lifting your heart and mind to God. It does not need special words; you can talk to God as you would to someone who loves you. Saint Thérèse of Lisieux called prayer "a surge of the heart, a simple look turned toward heaven."

Catholics pray in many ways: in our own words, with traditional prayers like the Our Father, with the Bible, in silence, and together at Mass. Traditional prayers are helpful when we do not know what to say; they have been prayed by millions of people before us.
When the disciples asked Jesus, "Lord, teach us to pray," he gave them the Our Father. It is the perfect place to start. Try praying it slowly once a day this week, thinking about each line.

A simple daily habit: when you wake up, make the Sign of the Cross and offer your day to God. Before sleep, think back over the day, thank God for one good thing, and say sorry for anything you regret.
sessions.reflection: What would help you make a few minutes of prayer part of your day?

sessions.title: The journey of faith: the Trinity, faith, and the God who is love
sessions.summary: God made us out of love, to share his life. He has shown us who he is: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

sources.title: Psalm 23, The Lord is my shepherd

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 1
lesson: This session opens with Psalm 23, "The Lord is my shepherd," alongside a picture of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus. Both say the same thing: we are not walking alone. God goes ahead of us, walks beside us, and leads us home.
## Made by love, for love
God did not need to create us. He is perfectly happy and complete in himself. He made us freely, out of pure goodness, so that we could share in his own blessed life (Catechism 1, 293).
That is why every human heart carries a longing that nothing in this world fully satisfies. We were made by the God who is love, and we are made for his love (Catechism 27-30).
> Our hearts are restless until they rest in you. — St. Augustine

And God is not waiting for us to find our own way to him. At every moment of our lives he comes close, calling us to seek him, to know him and to love him (Catechism 1). Like the shepherd of Psalm 23, he is the one who comes looking for us.
## One God, three Persons

There is only one God (Catechism 200-202). Yet God has revealed that his one life is a communion of three Persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Catechism 221). We could never have worked this out on our own. We know it because God showed us, by sending his Son, Jesus, and then his Holy Spirit.

This is God's "inmost secret": his very being is love shared between Persons. As the Catechism says, God himself is an eternal exchange of love, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and he has made us to share in that exchange (Catechism 221).

The diagram below, sometimes called the Shield of the Trinity, helps keep this straight. Each Person is fully God. But the Persons are truly distinct: the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is not the Father.
[[figure:trinity]]

So we must avoid two mistakes. It is not three gods working together, and it is not one God simply wearing three masks. The Church worships one God in the Trinity, without mixing up the Persons or dividing God's one being. Their glory is equal and their majesty is eternal (Catechism 266).
## What faith is
Faith is our answer to the God who has made himself known. It has two sides (Catechism 150).
- Intellect: with our minds we believe, saying yes to what God has revealed.
- Will: with our hearts we choose to entrust our whole lives to him, the way you would trust a friend with everything.
[[figure:faith]]
Faith is not only agreeing with ideas, and it is not only a feeling. It is both: knowing who God is, and choosing to lean on him.
## Three key elements of prayer
Prayer is how faith becomes a relationship. Three simple elements can shape it:
- Praise: start by focusing on God, not on your problems. This is the "truth zone": God is in control and he loves you. Tell him you love him too.
- Petition: ask for what you and others need. Nothing is too small to bring to him.
- Forgiveness: ask God to forgive your sins, and choose to forgive the people who have hurt you.

> We must speak to God as a friend speaks to his friend, as a servant to his master; now asking some favor, now acknowledging our faults, and communicating to him all that concerns us: our thoughts, our fears, our projects, our desires, and in all things seeking his counsel. — St. Ignatius of Loyola
sessions.reflection: Pray Psalm 23 slowly this week. Where in your life do you need to trust that God is the shepherd walking with you?

deeper.title: Why two creeds?
deeper.text:
A creed is a short summary of what Christians believe. The Church keeps two from the early centuries, and both proclaim faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

The Apostles' Creed is one of the earliest, first used in Rome when people were baptized. We still use it at Baptisms and to begin the Rosary.

The Nicene Creed was first written at the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD to answer questions that had arisen about the Trinity and about whether Jesus is truly God. Its extra detail is about clarity. It is the creed we normally say at Sunday Mass and on major feasts.
